verdict.reasoning: Patient says he has not much appetite and energy and is feeling down: "I've been feeling down and I didn't really have energy" and "I'm having a loss of appetite... I'm not eating very much."

He reports shortness of breath and symptoms in the lift: "Feel like I'm feeling short of breath..." and "when I go into the lift... my heart starts beating and I can't really breathe," indicating palpitations and SOB in that (enclosed) setting.
He describes low mood and reluctance to label it depression: "Now that I've been feeling down" and when asked "Would you say you're depressed?" he replies "You never want to say that, do you?"

They agree on about a stone over about 6 months: patient: "less than a stone"; clinician: "So. About a stone? ... six months. Okay. Okay. Six kilos." Thus ~6 kg over 6 months is a reasonable restatement.
He links low appetite, low energy and feeling down: "I've been feeling down and I didn't really have energy" and later notes loss of appetite.
Shortness of breath is reported, especially related to lifts: "Feel like I'm feeling short of breath" and "when I go into the lift... my heart starts beating and I can't really breathe."

He feels his heart racing with shortness of breath: "my heart starts beating. I feel like I can't breathe" and clinician clarifies palpitations: "You're describing, like, palpitations to me" with patient agreeing "Yeah."
He reports low mood and possible depression: "I've been feeling down" and equivocates when asked if he is depressed: "You never want to say that, do you?"

Time course and amount are discussed: they settle on about a stone (~6 kg) over roughly six months: "Roughly six months. Would you say" / "Something like that?" and "About a stone?... six months. Okay. Okay. Six kilos."
Loss of appetite is present along with weight loss: "I'm having a loss of appetite. Yeah, I'm not eating very much" and later they discuss ongoing weight loss over months, implying association.
He reports nausea without vomiting: "I feel nauseous. Every now and again" and when asked "Have you been ever sick with it?" replies "No, actually not."

He denies bowel habit changes: "How are your bowels?" / "That's okay. I would say I don't really have problems when going to the toilet." and no diarrhea or blood: "No, no diarrhea?... no blood in the poo?" / "No, no."
He has a history of underactive thyroid: "Yes. I had too little activity of my thyroid" and clinician confirms "Oh, yeah. Underactive thyroid? Yes."
He previously took thyroxine for this: "And in that I took thyroxine."
He has stopped since changing jobs: "Are you using it every day?" / "Not anymore." and "I have not been taking it in the last. Actually, since I changed law firm, I would say."

No physical exam or vitals are performed; the clinician explicitly says a physical exam will be later: "we would need to do a physical examination" and "there's nothing from what you history... we urgently warrant a physical examination at this point." No vitals are mentioned.
Hypothyroidism is mentioned as past history but not explicitly assessed as an active current problem; there is no statement such as adding it to an active problem list.

The clinician notes temporal coincidence but does not state that stopping thyroxine is contributing to symptoms: "So all these things are since you've stopped taking the thyroxine." Patient says "that might be coinciding. I'm not sure." No explicit causal link to fatigue or mood is made.
Weight loss is discussed but not clearly framed as a distinct, separate problem from appetite and general low energy in an assessment statement.

While gradual weight loss over ~6 months and appetite loss are described, the clinician does not explicitly note in an assessment that weight loss is gradual and associated with appetite loss; this phrasing is an inferred assessment not present in the transcript.
Shortness of breath and palpitations are discussed as symptoms, but the clinician does not explicitly state them as a separate assessed problem in the way documented.
The clinician asks about stress in general but does not explicitly question whether stress or anxiety is related specifically to the lift-associated palpitations and shortness of breath.

Clinician plans a general set of bloods including several components: "we'll just do a general set of bloods where we look at things like anemia, how your kidney functions are, your livers, all that with vitamin levels" and given context of underactive thyroid, this implies thyroid function as part of the workup.

He is told to seek urgent care for chest pain or bowel changes: "with palpitations or chest pain... you need to go to A and E" and later "if your, you know, bowels change... you need to get in touch with us."
The clinician describes coordinating via support to arrange blood tests: "you need to ring up support and I'll do the form for you... so that we can organize that blood test for you."
Follow-up after blood results is planned: "once you get the result, you will receive a text message... to tell you to book an appointment."
He is told to recontact if worse: "If you're feeling poorly, don't wait for that. Just get in touch with us again."
Follow-up after blood tests is advised: "once you get the result, you will receive a text message through your phone to tell you to book an appointment."

He is advised to contact the team if things worsen or specific symptoms arise: "If you're feeling poorly, don't wait for that. Just get in touch with us again" and earlier "with palpitations or chest pain... you need to go to A and E" and "if your... bowels change... you need to get in touch with us."
